questions.q: In the catalog Dockerfile's runtime stage, what does `USER catalog` accomplish?
options: It creates the catalog database user inside Postgres
It switches the active user for the rest of the Dockerfile and the running container, so the process doesn't run as root
It renames the image to "catalog"
It tells Compose which service this Dockerfile belongs to
questions.explain: `USER catalog` switches the effective user from root to the dedicated `catalog` account created earlier with `useradd`, so the container's main process runs non-root.

questions.q: What does `depends_on: catalog-db: condition: service_healthy` do for the checkout service?
options: It deletes catalog-db if checkout fails to start
It delays starting checkout until catalog-db's health check actually passes, not just until catalog-db starts
It makes checkout and catalog-db share the same container
It has no real effect outside of swarm mode
questions.explain: The `service_healthy` condition ties startup order to the dependency's health check result, not just its process starting -- so checkout waits for a database that's genuinely ready to accept connections.

questions.q: Why can `checkout` reach the database at the hostname `catalog-db` instead of needing its IP address?
options: Because catalog-db is hardcoded into the checkout image
Because every container shares the host's /etc/hosts file by default
Because both services sit on the same user-defined network, where Docker's embedded DNS resolves service names automatically
Because `mem_limit` enables name resolution
questions.explain: On a user-defined network like `northbridge-net`, Docker runs embedded DNS that resolves each service's name to its current container IP, so services can reach each other by name.

questions.q: Why is `catalog-db-data` declared under `volumes:` and mounted into catalog-db, rather than left as part of the container's own filesystem?
options: So the database's data persists independently of the catalog-db container's lifecycle
So the image builds faster
Named volumes are required for a healthcheck to work
It has no practical effect and is purely cosmetic
questions.explain: A named volume lives outside any single container's writable layer. catalog-db's data directory survives `docker compose down` and container recreation because it's stored in the volume, not in the container itself.

questions.q: After `docker compose up -d`, what does seeing `catalog-db` and `catalog` listed as "Up (healthy)" in `docker compose ps` confirm?
options: That the images were pulled from a registry rather than built locally
That those services' health checks have actually passed, not just that their processes started
That resource limits have been removed
That the .env file was committed to the repo
questions.explain: The "(healthy)" status only appears once a service's configured `healthcheck` succeeds -- it's a stronger signal than "Up" alone, which just means the container's process started.
